{{Hindu philosophy}}
'''Jayanta Bhatta''' ({{circa|820}} CE – {{circa|900}} CE<ref name="Hegde" />) was a poet, teacher, logician, and an advisor to King [[Sankaravarman]] of [[Kashmir]]. He was a philosopher of the [[Nyaya]] school of [[Hindu philosophy]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Francis Clooney|title=Hindu God, Christian God: How Reason Helps Break Down the Boundaries Between Religions|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ub0VDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA39|year=2010|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-973872-4|pages=39–40}}</ref><ref name="csaba15">{{cite book|author1=Bhatta Jayanta|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kigTCgAAQBAJ|title=Much Ado about Religion|author2=Csaba Dezsö|publisher=New York University Press|year=2005|isbn=978-0-8147-1979-4|pages=15–17}}</ref> He authored three works on [[Nyaya|Nyāya]] philosophy: one of which is not known, an allegorical drama, and a commentary on [[Pāṇini|Pāṇinian grammar]], He refutes the arguments given by [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] philosophers like [[Dharmakirti]] and [[Dignāga]] against the [[Vedas]] and establishes the authority of the [[Vedas]].<ref name="Hegde" />

==Early life==
Jayanta was born into a wealthy [[Gaur Brahmins|Gaur Brahmin]] family.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="csaba15" /> He was a [[child prodigy]], composing a commentary to [[Pāṇini|Panini]]'s ''[[Ashtadhyayi]]'' and earned the name Nava-Vrittikara, or new commentator.<ref name="agama" /> Later in life, he mastered various ''[[shastra]]'' and ''[[Agama (Hinduism)|agama]]'', distinguished himself in scholarly debates, and passed his knowledge on to his students.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}}

Jayanta's birth year, lifespan, dates of his written works are a subject of scholarly debates.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}} His philosophical work ''Nyāyamañjarī'' as well as his drama ''[[Āgamaḍambara]]'', refer to King [[Sankaravarman]] (883 – 902 CE) as a contemporary.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}}

''Kādambarikathāsāra'', a work written by Jayanta's son Abhinanda, mentions that Jayanta's great grandfather was a minister of king [[Lalitaditya Muktapida]], who was a ruler of the Karkota dynasty in the second quarter of the 8th century CE.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}} Several attempts to specify his life span are based on references to his work by other authors and references to contemporary events and individuals in his work. They range from the middle of the 8th century CE to the start of the 10th century CE. However, most reliable estimates place him around the 9th century CE.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}}

===Lineage===
''Kādambarikathāsāra'' provides some information about Jayanta's lineage. It says his ancestor Shakti was a [[Gaur Brahmins|Gaur Brahmin]] and a direct [[patriline]] descendant of [[Bharadwaja]] gotra from the [[Bengal]], who lived in Darvabhisara, near the border of [[Kashmir]]. His son was named Mitra, and his grandson was Saktisvämin (Shaktisvamin).<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Kumara Varkey |url=http://archive.org/details/encyclopediaofindianphilosophyvolume02traditionofnyayavaisesikauptogangesakarlpotterh._415_E |title=Encyclopedia Of Indian Philosophy Volume 02 Tradition Of Nyaya Vaisesika Up To Gangesa Karl Potter H.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sharma |first=Rakhi |date=15 August 2022 |title=Evolution of Shaivaite Philosophic Tradition during Early Medieval Kashmir |url=https://d1wqtxts1xzle7.cloudfront.net/97451291/69_74_Evolution_of_Shaivaite_Philosophic_Tradition_during_Early_Medieval_Kashmir-libre.pdf?1674025345=&response-content-disposition=inline%3B+filename%3DEvolution_of_Shaivaite_Philosophic_Tradi.pdf&Expires=1719211437&Signature=ft0H306p~Rg3u4nPz8l7pmjMdLHUpW7UA9fMp0vkaea3p1ZjIfdBwt2lOXpXpsNt9RvrcYzbPo5GYeO0e2mv6yAQiu8aBfeg3s7HgVgJ~xCgAlsVYItgh8wFAKx3K0wDOmhu2zDCs313PZqv1ESSo-d4gLSjG~WJEVdWPUnHkKBn5p4MYsAzQqWPNMAuL4gKpdL8Nm3qkRP2B4Lyjucn1WA0kz~JD6l8~B3wwbdiDU~otLd3-A9MWQGkKSpBXL-DlgkP4-tmRqNmEV9fv3B~5ZrBfs56VruoIbadbEauREm~0VIhZPkkTGiU9tirYtrL42PVvaB0hUxsZYvWUAS8GA__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAJLOHF5GGSLRBV4ZA |journal=Central Asian Journal of Social Sciences and History |volume=3 |issue=10 |pages=71 |via=Academia}}</ref>

Saktisvämin, the great grandfather of Jayanta, was a minister of Kashmir [[Lalitaditya Muktapida]] of the Karkota dynasty ({{circa|724}} – 761 CE). Jayanta mentions in ''Nyayamanjari'' that his grandfather obtained a village named Gauramulaka, believed to have been located north of the modern town of [[Rajouri]], from King Muktapida. Saktisvämin had a son named Chandra, Jayanta's father.<ref name="agama">{{cite web|url=http://www.claysanskritlibrary.org/excerpts/CSLMuchAdoIntro.pdf.zip|title=Introduction to Agamadambara|author=Csaba Dezso|access-date=19 June 2007|archive-date=10 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160410005134/http://claysanskritlibrary.org/excerpts/CSLMuchAdoIntro.pdf.zip|url-status=dead}}</ref>

== Career ==
The ''[[Agamadambara]]'' provides details about Bhatta's political career.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}} He was an adviser to Kashmiri king [[Sankaravarman]]. In his position, he played a role in banishing the Nilambara (Black-Blankets) sect from Kashmir.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}} Commenting on [[Tantric sex|Tantric literature]], he argued that the Nilambara sect promoted "immoral teachings". Jayanta claimed the Nilambara "wear simply one blue garment, and then as a group engages in unconstrained public sex". He argued that this practice was "unnecessary" and threatened the fundamental values of society.<ref>{{cite book|last=Flood|first=Gavin D.|author-link=Gavin Flood|title=The Tantric Body, The Secret Tradition of Hindu Religion|publisher=I.B Taurus|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1Uer8W670IoC|year=2006|isbn=978-1-84511-011-6|pages=48–49}}</ref>

== Works ==

===Philosophical works===
Jayanta wrote three known treatises on [[Nyaya]] philosophy, of which two survive.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}} His first, the ''Nyayamanjari'' (A Cluster of Flowers of the Nyaya tree) is a commentary on Nyaya-aphorisms that serves as a critique of the theories of rival philosophical systems like the [[Mīmāṃsā|Mīmānsādarśana]].{{citation needed|date= August 2022}}

His second, the ''Nyayakalika'' (A Bud of the Nyaya tree) is an overview of the basic tenets of the [[Nyāya Sūtras]], a foundational text of the Nyaya school.  His third work, ''Pallava'' (probably ''Nyayapallava'', A Twig of the Nyaya tree) though quoted in ''Syadvadaratnakara'', has not survived.<ref name="Hegde" /><ref name="agama" />

Jayanta mentions in ''Nyayamanjari'' that he wrote this treatise during his confinement in a cave by the king.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jha |first=V N |url=https://archive.org/details/nyayamanjariahnikaivnjha_202003_952_v |title=Nyayamanjari of Jayantabhatta (Ahnika-I) |date=1995 |pages=iii}}</ref> This treatise is unique because it is an independent work, not a commentary of an earlier work.{{citation needed|date= August 2022}}

Secondly, according to Jayanta, the purpose of Nyaya is to protect the authority of the ''[[Vedas]]'', Hinduism's oldest scriptures, whereas earlier Nyaya scholars considered Nyaya to be an ''[[Anviksiki|Anvikshiki]]'' (scientific study) providing true knowledge about the real nature of the objects of cognition.

==== Nyayamanjari ====
Jayanta, in his Nyayamanjari, identifies ignorance (''[[Mohā|moha]]''), attachment (''[[Raga (Sanskrit term)|raga]]''), and antipathy ([[dvesha]]) as three distinct defects (''dosas'') that drive human actions:<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Dasgupta |first=Surendranath |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.461620/page/n423/mode/2up |title=A History Of Indian Philosophy Vol. 2 |date=1923 |publication-date=413}}</ref>

* ''moha'': further includes ''dosas'' such as ''[[Pramāda|pramada]]'' (carelessness), ''mada'' (sense of false superiority)
* ''raga'': further includes ''dosas'' such as ''[[kama]]'', ''[[trsna]]'' (desire)
* ''dvesha'': further includes ''dosas'' such as ''droha'' (harming others), ''[[Īrṣyā|irsya]]'' (jealousy)
Jayanta considers ''moha'' as the worst defect arguing that it gives rise to ''raga'' and ''dvesha''. He further argues that all defects stem from false knowledge and are resolved by right knowledge, however, each defect is psychologically distinct.<ref name=":1" />

=== Literary works ===
His major literary work is ''{{IAST|[[Āgamaḍambara]]}}'', a Sanskrit play in four acts. The hero of his quasi-philosophical drama is a young graduate of the [[Mimansa]] school, who wants to defeat all opponents of Vedas through reasoning.<ref name="agama" />

== Philosophy ==

=== God ===
The discussion of God's Existence is found in part 1 of ''Nyaya Manjuri''. Jayanta adheres to a realist viewpoint of God and the world and defends the possibility of reasoned arguments favoring God as a realistic and adequate cause of the world.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Clooney|first=Francis Xavier|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ub0VDAAAQBAJ|title=Hindu God, Christian God: How Reason Helps Break Down the Boundaries Between Religions|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|year=2010|pages=39–45|isbn=978-0-19-973872-4}}</ref>

=== Criticism of Lokayats ===
Jayanta Bhatta criticized the [[Charvaka|Lokayata]] school of philosophy for not developing a Lokayata culture. He said, "The Lokayata is not an [[Agama (Hinduism)|Agama]]. viz. not a guide to cultural living, not a system of do's and dont's; hence it is nothing but irresponsible wrangling."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Narain|first=Harsh|url=https://archive.org/details/MythOfCompositeCultureHarshNarain/page/n33/mode/1up?q=The+Lokayata+is+not+an+Agama.+viz.+not+a+guide+to+cultural+living%2C+not+a+system+of+do%27s+and+don%E2%80%99ts%3B+hence+it+is+nothing+but+irresponsible+wrangling+++|title=Myths of Composite Culture and Equality of Religions|year=1990|pages=33–34}}</ref>

==English translations==
{{main|List of Sanskrit plays in English translation}}
The [[Clay Sanskrit Library]] published a translation of ''{{IAST|[[Āgamaḍambara]]}}'' by Csaba Dezső under the title of ''Much Ado about Religion''.
